title: Moral beauty
hook: seeing great goodness gives a warm lift psychologists call elevation (Haidt)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul Piff's grove of eucalyptus and a handful of dropped pens. Your line was tall trees. Today, an awe that comes not from trees or stars, but from people.

Snow overnight. At six in the morning a teenager from down the street is already out with a shovel, clearing the driveway of the elderly woman next door. No one asked. No one is filming. He finishes, leans the shovel by her steps, and walks home. Some people who see a moment like that describe a warmth spreading in the chest, a lump in the throat, a sudden wish to go and do something good themselves. That reaction has a name, and a psychologist went looking for it.
screen: `SNOW, A SHOVEL, NO ONE ASKED.` → `A WARMTH IN THE CHEST.` → `A REACTION WITH A NAME.`

segments.voice: The psychologist is Jonathan Haidt, and the name he gave it is elevation. First, what it is. Elevation is the response to seeing someone act with unusual goodness: kindness, courage, generosity, forgiveness. Haidt calls that goodness moral beauty: beauty in a deed instead of a sunset. Second, what it feels like, as people describe it. A warm or glowing feeling in the chest. Sometimes tears. A sense of being lifted, opened. Haidt set it beside disgust as its opposite: disgust is the feeling of watching people sink below the ordinary, and elevation the feeling of watching someone rise above it. Third, what it does. In Haidt's research, people who felt elevation reported wanting to help others and to become better people themselves. Goodness, seen, seems to be catching. In Haidt's account the feeling points outward, toward other people and toward the person the watcher would like to be. Fourth, an old teacher who knew this. Marcus Aurelius, the Roman emperor who wrote private notes to himself, kept a habit of thinking about the good in the people around him. In George Long's translation: "When thou wishest to delight thyself, think of the virtues of those who live with thee." He didn't call it elevation. He used it as medicine: when he wanted delight, he went looking for someone's goodness on purpose. Moral beauty doesn't need a headline. It turns up on ordinary streets, in small doses, for anyone watching for it.
screen: `MORAL BEAUTY: GOODNESS IN A DEED.` · `A WARMTH IN THE CHEST.` · `IT MAKES PEOPLE WANT TO HELP.` · `MARCUS LOOKS FOR VIRTUES.` · then, large: `THINK OF THE VIRTUES OF THOSE WHO LIVE WITH THEE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one great kindness you've seen, read about or received, and go to the moment itself: the hands, the faces, what was said. Stay with it for a few breaths and notice whether anything moves in your chest or your throat, and whether it asks anything of you. If you pray, you can give thanks for that person in your own way.
Moral beauty. Unusual goodness, seen in a person's deed. Seeing it, some people describe a warm lift that Jonathan Haidt calls elevation. Today's word.
Your line: elevation. A good deed can lift the one who only watched it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some people deliberately seek out stories of great kindness, or recall the virtues of people they know, as a way to lift themselves and to prompt their own good deeds; Marcus Aurelius describes doing this in his Meditations.

chat.says: Why do I tear up watching a stranger do something kind?
options: Haidt calls it elevation: seeing moral beauty can warm the chest and make us want to help.
Haidt says it's guilt, because seeing kindness reminds us of what we didn't do.
Haidt says it's just tiredness; strong feelings come out when we're worn down.
chat.meaning: Haidt calls it elevation, the response to moral beauty: a warm feeling in the chest, sometimes tears, and a wish to help others and become better.
